title: Economics: Micro and Macro Principles

sources.name: Original educational wording based on general subject knowledge

description: For learners reviewing economics: scarcity, markets, incentives, market failures, firms, national output, employment, prices, and policy. Definitions are paired with applied examples.

cards.front: What is scarcity?
cards.back: Resources are limited relative to the uses people want to make of them.
cards.example: A town cannot fund every proposed public project with its available resources.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A town cannot fund every proposed public project with its available resources.
cards.back: Scarcity: Resources are limited relative to the uses people want to make of them.
cards.example: A town cannot fund every proposed public project with its available resources.

cards.front: What is opportunity cost?
cards.back: The value of the best alternative forgone when a choice is made.
cards.example: Choosing an extra work shift means giving up the most valued alternative use of that time.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Choosing an extra work shift means giving up the most valued alternative use of that time.
cards.back: Opportunity cost: The value of the best alternative forgone when a choice is made.
cards.example: Choosing an extra work shift means giving up the most valued alternative use of that time.

cards.front: What is marginal analysis?
cards.back: Comparing the additional benefit and additional cost of a small change in an activity.
cards.example: A bakery considers whether selling one more batch would add more revenue than cost.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A bakery considers whether selling one more batch would add more revenue than cost.
cards.back: Marginal analysis: Comparing the additional benefit and additional cost of a small change in an activity.
cards.example: A bakery considers whether selling one more batch would add more revenue than cost.

cards.front: What is sunk cost?
cards.back: A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered and should not determine a forward-looking choice.
cards.example: A nonrefundable ticket payment cannot be changed by deciding whether to attend now.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A nonrefundable ticket payment cannot be changed by deciding whether to attend now.
cards.back: Sunk cost: A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered and should not determine a forward-looking choice.
cards.example: A nonrefundable ticket payment cannot be changed by deciding whether to attend now.

cards.front: What is incentive?
cards.back: A change in expected benefits or costs that can influence behavior.
cards.example: A per-bag trash fee encourages households to reduce discarded waste.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A per-bag trash fee encourages households to reduce discarded waste.
cards.back: Incentive: A change in expected benefits or costs that can influence behavior.
cards.example: A per-bag trash fee encourages households to reduce discarded waste.

cards.front: What is production possibilities frontier?
cards.back: The boundary of combinations of outputs an economy can produce with available resources and technology.
cards.example: A graph shows the maximum feasible combinations of wheat and cloth.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A graph shows the maximum feasible combinations of wheat and cloth.
cards.back: Production possibilities frontier: The boundary of combinations of outputs an economy can produce with available resources and technology.
cards.example: A graph shows the maximum feasible combinations of wheat and cloth.

cards.front: What is productive efficiency?
cards.back: Producing output with no avoidable waste of inputs, given available technology.
cards.example: A factory cannot make more of one good without reducing another with its current resources.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A factory cannot make more of one good without reducing another with its current resources.
cards.back: Productive efficiency: Producing output with no avoidable waste of inputs, given available technology.
cards.example: A factory cannot make more of one good without reducing another with its current resources.

cards.front: What is comparative advantage?
cards.back: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
cards.example: One country gives up fewer tons of wheat per car produced than another country.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? One country gives up fewer tons of wheat per car produced than another country.
cards.back: Comparative advantage: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
cards.example: One country gives up fewer tons of wheat per car produced than another country.

cards.front: What is absolute advantage?
cards.back: The ability to produce more output with the same inputs, or the same output with fewer inputs.
cards.example: One worker assembles more chairs per hour than another using comparable tools.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? One worker assembles more chairs per hour than another using comparable tools.
cards.back: Absolute advantage: The ability to produce more output with the same inputs, or the same output with fewer inputs.
cards.example: One worker assembles more chairs per hour than another using comparable tools.

cards.front: What is specialization?
cards.back: Concentrating production on a narrower set of tasks or goods.
cards.example: Workers focus on separate stages of assembly instead of each making an entire product.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Workers focus on separate stages of assembly instead of each making an entire product.
cards.back: Specialization: Concentrating production on a narrower set of tasks or goods.
cards.example: Workers focus on separate stages of assembly instead of each making an entire product.

cards.front: What is demand?
cards.back: The relationship between a good's price and quantities buyers are willing and able to purchase, other things equal.
cards.example: A schedule lists how many apples buyers would purchase at several possible prices.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A schedule lists how many apples buyers would purchase at several possible prices.
cards.back: Demand: The relationship between a good's price and quantities buyers are willing and able to purchase, other things equal.
cards.example: A schedule lists how many apples buyers would purchase at several possible prices.

cards.front: What is law of demand?
cards.back: Other things equal, a higher own price generally reduces quantity demanded.
cards.example: Consumers buy fewer oranges after the price of oranges rises, with other factors unchanged.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Consumers buy fewer oranges after the price of oranges rises, with other factors unchanged.
cards.back: Law of demand: Other things equal, a higher own price generally reduces quantity demanded.
cards.example: Consumers buy fewer oranges after the price of oranges rises, with other factors unchanged.

cards.front: What is supply?
cards.back: The relationship between a good's price and quantities sellers are willing and able to offer, other things equal.
cards.example: Farmers report how many bushels they would sell at different wheat prices.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Farmers report how many bushels they would sell at different wheat prices.
cards.back: Supply: The relationship between a good's price and quantities sellers are willing and able to offer, other things equal.
cards.example: Farmers report how many bushels they would sell at different wheat prices.

cards.front: What is law of supply?
cards.back: Other things equal, a higher own price generally increases quantity supplied.
cards.example: Producers offer more strawberries when strawberry prices rise, with production conditions unchanged.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Producers offer more strawberries when strawberry prices rise, with production conditions unchanged.
cards.back: Law of supply: Other things equal, a higher own price generally increases quantity supplied.
cards.example: Producers offer more strawberries when strawberry prices rise, with production conditions unchanged.

cards.front: What is market equilibrium?
cards.back: A price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
cards.example: At one price, buyers want exactly the quantity sellers offer.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? At one price, buyers want exactly the quantity sellers offer.
cards.back: Market equilibrium: A price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
cards.example: At one price, buyers want exactly the quantity sellers offer.

cards.front: What is shortage?
cards.back: A situation in which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price.
cards.example: At a low posted ticket price, more tickets are wanted than are available.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? At a low posted ticket price, more tickets are wanted than are available.
cards.back: Shortage: A situation in which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price.
cards.example: At a low posted ticket price, more tickets are wanted than are available.

cards.front: What is surplus?
cards.back: A situation in which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the current price.
cards.example: At a high posted price, some produce remains unsold because sellers offer more than buyers want.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? At a high posted price, some produce remains unsold because sellers offer more than buyers want.
cards.back: Surplus: A situation in which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the current price.
cards.example: At a high posted price, some produce remains unsold because sellers offer more than buyers want.

cards.front: What is demand shift?
cards.back: A change in quantities demanded at given prices caused by a nonprice determinant of demand.
cards.example: A rise in population increases housing demand at each possible rent.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A rise in population increases housing demand at each possible rent.
cards.back: Demand shift: A change in quantities demanded at given prices caused by a nonprice determinant of demand.
cards.example: A rise in population increases housing demand at each possible rent.

cards.front: What is movement along a demand curve?
cards.back: A change in quantity demanded caused by a change in the good's own price, with other demand determinants fixed.
cards.example: A lower coffee price increases purchases along an unchanged coffee demand curve.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A lower coffee price increases purchases along an unchanged coffee demand curve.
cards.back: Movement along a demand curve: A change in quantity demanded caused by a change in the good's own price, with other demand determinants fixed.
cards.example: A lower coffee price increases purchases along an unchanged coffee demand curve.

cards.front: What is normal good?
cards.back: A good whose demand rises when consumer income rises, other things equal.
cards.example: Higher household income increases demand for a particular kind of restaurant meal.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Higher household income increases demand for a particular kind of restaurant meal.
cards.back: Normal good: A good whose demand rises when consumer income rises, other things equal.
cards.example: Higher household income increases demand for a particular kind of restaurant meal.

cards.front: What is inferior good?
cards.back: A good whose demand falls when consumer income rises, other things equal.
cards.example: As income rises, some households buy less of a particular low-cost staple in favor of alternatives.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? As income rises, some households buy less of a particular low-cost staple in favor of alternatives.
cards.back: Inferior good: A good whose demand falls when consumer income rises, other things equal.
cards.example: As income rises, some households buy less of a particular low-cost staple in favor of alternatives.

cards.front: What are substitutes?
cards.back: Goods for which a rise in the price of one tends to increase demand for the other.
cards.example: A higher tea price leads some consumers to demand more coffee.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A higher tea price leads some consumers to demand more coffee.
cards.back: Substitutes: Goods for which a rise in the price of one tends to increase demand for the other.
cards.example: A higher tea price leads some consumers to demand more coffee.

cards.front: What are complements?
cards.back: Goods for which a rise in the price of one tends to reduce demand for the other.
cards.example: More expensive printers can reduce demand for compatible ink cartridges.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? More expensive printers can reduce demand for compatible ink cartridges.
cards.back: Complements: Goods for which a rise in the price of one tends to reduce demand for the other.
cards.example: More expensive printers can reduce demand for compatible ink cartridges.

cards.front: What is price elasticity of demand?
cards.back: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price; its magnitude measures responsiveness.
cards.example: A small percentage price change produces a much larger percentage change in purchases.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A small percentage price change produces a much larger percentage change in purchases.
cards.back: Price elasticity of demand: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price; its magnitude measures responsiveness.
cards.example: A small percentage price change produces a much larger percentage change in purchases.

cards.front: What is price-inelastic demand?
cards.back: Demand with an elasticity magnitude below one over the relevant range.
cards.example: A 10 percent price increase causes quantity demanded to fall by only 2 percent.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A 10 percent price increase causes quantity demanded to fall by only 2 percent.
cards.back: Price-inelastic demand: Demand with an elasticity magnitude below one over the relevant range.
cards.example: A 10 percent price increase causes quantity demanded to fall by only 2 percent.

cards.front: What is price-elastic demand?
cards.back: Demand with an elasticity magnitude above one over the relevant range.
cards.example: A 5 percent price increase causes quantity demanded to fall by 15 percent.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A 5 percent price increase causes quantity demanded to fall by 15 percent.
cards.back: Price-elastic demand: Demand with an elasticity magnitude above one over the relevant range.
cards.example: A 5 percent price increase causes quantity demanded to fall by 15 percent.

cards.front: What is consumer surplus?
cards.back: The difference between buyers' willingness to pay and what they actually pay, summed over purchased units.
cards.example: A buyer willing to pay 30 pays 20 and receives a surplus of 10.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A buyer willing to pay 30 pays 20 and receives a surplus of 10.
cards.back: Consumer surplus: The difference between buyers' willingness to pay and what they actually pay, summed over purchased units.
cards.example: A buyer willing to pay 30 pays 20 and receives a surplus of 10.

cards.front: What is producer surplus?
cards.back: The difference between revenue received and the minimum amount sellers would accept for supplied units.
cards.example: A seller receives 12 for a unit that it would have supplied for 8.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A seller receives 12 for a unit that it would have supplied for 8.
cards.back: Producer surplus: The difference between revenue received and the minimum amount sellers would accept for supplied units.
cards.example: A seller receives 12 for a unit that it would have supplied for 8.

cards.front: What is price ceiling?
cards.back: A legal maximum price; it is binding if set below the market-clearing price.
cards.example: A rule prevents a landlord from charging more than a specified rent.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A rule prevents a landlord from charging more than a specified rent.
cards.back: Price ceiling: A legal maximum price; it is binding if set below the market-clearing price.
cards.example: A rule prevents a landlord from charging more than a specified rent.

cards.front: What is price floor?
cards.back: A legal minimum price; it is binding if set above the market-clearing price.
cards.example: A rule prevents a commodity from being sold below a specified price.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A rule prevents a commodity from being sold below a specified price.
cards.back: Price floor: A legal minimum price; it is binding if set above the market-clearing price.
cards.example: A rule prevents a commodity from being sold below a specified price.

cards.front: What is tax incidence?
cards.back: The distribution of a tax's economic burden between buyers and sellers, influenced by relative elasticities.
cards.example: A tax legally collected from sellers partly raises the price paid by consumers.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A tax legally collected from sellers partly raises the price paid by consumers.
cards.back: Tax incidence: The distribution of a tax's economic burden between buyers and sellers, influenced by relative elasticities.
cards.example: A tax legally collected from sellers partly raises the price paid by consumers.

cards.front: What is deadweight loss?
cards.back: A loss of total economic surplus from trades or activities distorted away from an efficient level.
cards.example: A tax prevents some mutually beneficial trades from occurring.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A tax prevents some mutually beneficial trades from occurring.
cards.back: Deadweight loss: A loss of total economic surplus from trades or activities distorted away from an efficient level.
cards.example: A tax prevents some mutually beneficial trades from occurring.

cards.front: What is negative externality?
cards.back: A cost imposed on others that is not fully reflected in the decision-maker's private cost.
cards.example: A factory's emissions harm nearby residents without compensation.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A factory's emissions harm nearby residents without compensation.
cards.back: Negative externality: A cost imposed on others that is not fully reflected in the decision-maker's private cost.
cards.example: A factory's emissions harm nearby residents without compensation.

cards.front: What is positive externality?
cards.back: A benefit to others that is not fully reflected in the decision-maker's private benefit.
cards.example: A household's well-maintained garden improves neighbors' enjoyment of the street.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A household's well-maintained garden improves neighbors' enjoyment of the street.
cards.back: Positive externality: A benefit to others that is not fully reflected in the decision-maker's private benefit.
cards.example: A household's well-maintained garden improves neighbors' enjoyment of the street.

cards.front: What is public good?
cards.back: A good that is nonrival and nonexcludable in the relevant context.
cards.example: A warning siren alerts nearby residents without one person's hearing reducing another's access.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A warning siren alerts nearby residents without one person's hearing reducing another's access.
cards.back: Public good: A good that is nonrival and nonexcludable in the relevant context.
cards.example: A warning siren alerts nearby residents without one person's hearing reducing another's access.

cards.front: What is common resource?
cards.back: A rival resource from which excluding users is difficult.
cards.example: Fish in an open-access fishery can be depleted by individual catches.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Fish in an open-access fishery can be depleted by individual catches.
cards.back: Common resource: A rival resource from which excluding users is difficult.
cards.example: Fish in an open-access fishery can be depleted by individual catches.

cards.front: What is free-rider problem?
cards.back: People can benefit without paying, which can weaken incentives to provide a nonexcludable good.
cards.example: Residents hope others will finance a neighborhood benefit they can all enjoy.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Residents hope others will finance a neighborhood benefit they can all enjoy.
cards.back: Free-rider problem: People can benefit without paying, which can weaken incentives to provide a nonexcludable good.
cards.example: Residents hope others will finance a neighborhood benefit they can all enjoy.

cards.front: What is asymmetric information?
cards.back: One party to an interaction has relevant information that the other lacks.
cards.example: A used-car seller knows more about hidden defects than the buyer.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A used-car seller knows more about hidden defects than the buyer.
cards.back: Asymmetric information: One party to an interaction has relevant information that the other lacks.
cards.example: A used-car seller knows more about hidden defects than the buyer.

cards.front: What is adverse selection?
cards.back: Hidden information before an agreement causes the participating pool to differ in a way that can impair exchange.
cards.example: People expecting high claims are more inclined to buy a particular insurance policy.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? People expecting high claims are more inclined to buy a particular insurance policy.
cards.back: Adverse selection: Hidden information before an agreement causes the participating pool to differ in a way that can impair exchange.
cards.example: People expecting high claims are more inclined to buy a particular insurance policy.

cards.front: What is moral hazard?
cards.back: After an agreement, reduced exposure to consequences can change behavior in ways another party cannot fully observe.
cards.example: An insured person takes less care because some resulting losses are covered.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? An insured person takes less care because some resulting losses are covered.
cards.back: Moral hazard: After an agreement, reduced exposure to consequences can change behavior in ways another party cannot fully observe.
cards.example: An insured person takes less care because some resulting losses are covered.

cards.front: What is fixed cost?
cards.back: A cost that does not vary with current output over the relevant period.
cards.example: A shop pays the same monthly lease charge regardless of this week's sales.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A shop pays the same monthly lease charge regardless of this week's sales.
cards.back: Fixed cost: A cost that does not vary with current output over the relevant period.
cards.example: A shop pays the same monthly lease charge regardless of this week's sales.

cards.front: What is variable cost?
cards.back: A cost that changes as output changes.
cards.example: A bakery buys more flour when it produces more loaves.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A bakery buys more flour when it produces more loaves.
cards.back: Variable cost: A cost that changes as output changes.
cards.example: A bakery buys more flour when it produces more loaves.

cards.front: What is marginal cost?
cards.back: The additional cost of producing one more unit or a small additional amount of output.
cards.example: Making one additional table raises total cost by 40.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Making one additional table raises total cost by 40.
cards.back: Marginal cost: The additional cost of producing one more unit or a small additional amount of output.
cards.example: Making one additional table raises total cost by 40.

cards.front: What are economies of scale?
cards.back: A range in which long-run average cost falls as output increases.
cards.example: A larger plant spreads setup and specialization advantages across more units.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A larger plant spreads setup and specialization advantages across more units.
cards.back: Economies of scale: A range in which long-run average cost falls as output increases.
cards.example: A larger plant spreads setup and specialization advantages across more units.

cards.front: What is perfect competition?
cards.back: A market model with many price-taking firms selling a homogeneous good and free entry and exit.
cards.example: A small supplier in an idealized commodity market cannot profitably raise price above the market level.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A small supplier in an idealized commodity market cannot profitably raise price above the market level.
cards.back: Perfect competition: A market model with many price-taking firms selling a homogeneous good and free entry and exit.
cards.example: A small supplier in an idealized commodity market cannot profitably raise price above the market level.

cards.front: What is monopoly?
cards.back: A market structure with a single seller of a good lacking close substitutes, protected by entry barriers.
cards.example: One firm alone serves a market because rivals cannot legally or practically enter.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? One firm alone serves a market because rivals cannot legally or practically enter.
cards.back: Monopoly: A market structure with a single seller of a good lacking close substitutes, protected by entry barriers.
cards.example: One firm alone serves a market because rivals cannot legally or practically enter.

cards.front: What is oligopoly?
cards.back: A market structure dominated by a few firms whose choices affect one another.
cards.example: A small number of major producers consider rivals' reactions before changing prices.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A small number of major producers consider rivals' reactions before changing prices.
cards.back: Oligopoly: A market structure dominated by a few firms whose choices affect one another.
cards.example: A small number of major producers consider rivals' reactions before changing prices.

cards.front: What is monopolistic competition?
cards.back: A market structure with many firms selling differentiated products and relatively free entry and exit.
cards.example: Many restaurants compete while each offers a somewhat distinct product.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Many restaurants compete while each offers a somewhat distinct product.
cards.back: Monopolistic competition: A market structure with many firms selling differentiated products and relatively free entry and exit.
cards.example: Many restaurants compete while each offers a somewhat distinct product.

cards.front: What is nash equilibrium?
cards.back: A strategy profile in which no player can improve their payoff by changing only their own strategy.
cards.example: Each firm is choosing its best response to the other firm's current choice.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Each firm is choosing its best response to the other firm's current choice.
cards.back: Nash equilibrium: A strategy profile in which no player can improve their payoff by changing only their own strategy.
cards.example: Each firm is choosing its best response to the other firm's current choice.

cards.front: What is price discrimination?
cards.back: Charging different prices for reasons not fully explained by cost differences, often using willingness-to-pay differences.
cards.example: A seller offers group-specific prices for the same service.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A seller offers group-specific prices for the same service.
cards.back: Price discrimination: Charging different prices for reasons not fully explained by cost differences, often using willingness-to-pay differences.
cards.example: A seller offers group-specific prices for the same service.

cards.front: What is gross domestic product?
cards.back: The market value of final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a specified period.
cards.example: A newly produced domestic final good contributes to current domestic output.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A newly produced domestic final good contributes to current domestic output.
cards.back: Gross domestic product: The market value of final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a specified period.
cards.example: A newly produced domestic final good contributes to current domestic output.

cards.front: What is intermediate good?
cards.back: An input used in producing another good rather than purchased for final use.
cards.example: Flour purchased by a bakery becomes part of bread sold to consumers.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Flour purchased by a bakery becomes part of bread sold to consumers.
cards.back: Intermediate good: An input used in producing another good rather than purchased for final use.
cards.example: Flour purchased by a bakery becomes part of bread sold to consumers.

cards.front: What is value added?
cards.back: A producer's output value minus the value of intermediate inputs purchased from other producers.
cards.example: A bakery sells bread for 100 after buying intermediate ingredients for 40, adding 60 in value.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A bakery sells bread for 100 after buying intermediate ingredients for 40, adding 60 in value.
cards.back: Value added: A producer's output value minus the value of intermediate inputs purchased from other producers.
cards.example: A bakery sells bread for 100 after buying intermediate ingredients for 40, adding 60 in value.

cards.front: What is nominal gdp?
cards.back: GDP measured using prices prevailing in the period being measured.
cards.example: Total output value rises partly because current prices rise.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Total output value rises partly because current prices rise.
cards.back: Nominal GDP: GDP measured using prices prevailing in the period being measured.
cards.example: Total output value rises partly because current prices rise.

cards.front: What is real gdp?
cards.back: GDP adjusted to remove the effect of changes in the overall price level.
cards.example: An output measure aims to compare production across years while accounting for price changes.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? An output measure aims to compare production across years while accounting for price changes.
cards.back: Real GDP: GDP adjusted to remove the effect of changes in the overall price level.
cards.example: An output measure aims to compare production across years while accounting for price changes.

cards.front: What is gdp per capita?
cards.back: GDP divided by population; an average measure that does not show how income is distributed.
cards.example: Two countries with equal GDP can have different output per person because their populations differ.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Two countries with equal GDP can have different output per person because their populations differ.
cards.back: GDP per capita: GDP divided by population; an average measure that does not show how income is distributed.
cards.example: Two countries with equal GDP can have different output per person because their populations differ.

cards.front: What is economic growth?
cards.back: An increase in an economy's real output, often assessed over the long run or per person.
cards.example: An economy produces more real goods and services over successive years.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? An economy produces more real goods and services over successive years.
cards.back: Economic growth: An increase in an economy's real output, often assessed over the long run or per person.
cards.example: An economy produces more real goods and services over successive years.

cards.front: What is productivity?
cards.back: Output per unit of input, commonly output per hour worked.
cards.example: Workers produce more goods per hour after learning a more efficient method.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Workers produce more goods per hour after learning a more efficient method.
cards.back: Productivity: Output per unit of input, commonly output per hour worked.
cards.example: Workers produce more goods per hour after learning a more efficient method.

cards.front: What is business cycle?
cards.back: Fluctuations in aggregate economic activity around its longer-term path.
cards.example: A period of expansion is followed by a broad contraction and later recovery.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A period of expansion is followed by a broad contraction and later recovery.
cards.back: Business cycle: Fluctuations in aggregate economic activity around its longer-term path.
cards.example: A period of expansion is followed by a broad contraction and later recovery.

cards.front: What is recession?
cards.back: A significant, broad decline in economic activity lasting more than a brief interval; formal definitions vary.
cards.example: Output, employment, and income fall across much of an economy.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Output, employment, and income fall across much of an economy.
cards.back: Recession: A significant, broad decline in economic activity lasting more than a brief interval; formal definitions vary.
cards.example: Output, employment, and income fall across much of an economy.

cards.front: What is labor force?
cards.back: Employed people plus unemployed people who meet the relevant availability and job-search criteria.
cards.example: A person actively seeking work is counted together with those already employed.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A person actively seeking work is counted together with those already employed.
cards.back: Labor force: Employed people plus unemployed people who meet the relevant availability and job-search criteria.
cards.example: A person actively seeking work is counted together with those already employed.

cards.front: What is unemployment rate?
cards.back: The number of unemployed people divided by the labor force, multiplied by 100 percent.
cards.example: If 5 of 100 labor-force participants are unemployed, the rate is 5 percent.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? If 5 of 100 labor-force participants are unemployed, the rate is 5 percent.
cards.back: Unemployment rate: The number of unemployed people divided by the labor force, multiplied by 100 percent.
cards.example: If 5 of 100 labor-force participants are unemployed, the rate is 5 percent.

cards.front: What is labor-force participation rate?
cards.back: The labor force as a percentage of the relevant working-age population.
cards.example: Some adults leave job searching, reducing participation even if employment is unchanged.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Some adults leave job searching, reducing participation even if employment is unchanged.
cards.back: Labor-force participation rate: The labor force as a percentage of the relevant working-age population.
cards.example: Some adults leave job searching, reducing participation even if employment is unchanged.

cards.front: What is frictional unemployment?
cards.back: Unemployment associated with the time needed to match workers and jobs.
cards.example: A worker spends several weeks looking for a suitable job after moving cities.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A worker spends several weeks looking for a suitable job after moving cities.
cards.back: Frictional unemployment: Unemployment associated with the time needed to match workers and jobs.
cards.example: A worker spends several weeks looking for a suitable job after moving cities.

cards.front: What is structural unemployment?
cards.back: Unemployment arising from mismatches between workers and available jobs or persistent market structures.
cards.example: Workers' skills no longer match the skills sought in their region's expanding industries.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Workers' skills no longer match the skills sought in their region's expanding industries.
cards.back: Structural unemployment: Unemployment arising from mismatches between workers and available jobs or persistent market structures.
cards.example: Workers' skills no longer match the skills sought in their region's expanding industries.

cards.front: What is cyclical unemployment?
cards.back: Unemployment associated with insufficient aggregate demand during an economic downturn.
cards.example: Firms lay off workers after a broad decline in sales during a contraction.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? Firms lay off workers after a broad decline in sales during a contraction.
cards.back: Cyclical unemployment: Unemployment associated with insufficient aggregate demand during an economic downturn.

cards.front: What is inflation?
cards.back: A sustained increase in the general price level.
cards.example: The overall cost of a broad basket of goods and services rises over time.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? The overall cost of a broad basket of goods and services rises over time.
cards.back: Inflation: A sustained increase in the general price level.
cards.example: The overall cost of a broad basket of goods and services rises over time.

cards.front: What is deflation?
cards.back: A sustained decrease in the general price level.
cards.example: A broad price index falls over an extended period.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A broad price index falls over an extended period.
cards.back: Deflation: A sustained decrease in the general price level.
cards.example: A broad price index falls over an extended period.

cards.front: What is disinflation?
cards.back: A reduction in the rate of inflation; prices may still be rising.
cards.example: Inflation slows from 6 percent to 3 percent while the price level continues increasing.

cards.back: Disinflation: A reduction in the rate of inflation; prices may still be rising.

cards.front: What is consumer price index?
cards.back: An index tracking changes in prices paid by consumers for a defined basket of goods and services.
cards.example: A statistical agency follows prices of consumer purchases over time using basket weights.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A statistical agency follows prices of consumer purchases over time using basket weights.
cards.back: Consumer price index: An index tracking changes in prices paid by consumers for a defined basket of goods and services.

cards.front: What is real interest rate?
cards.back: An interest rate adjusted for inflation; approximately the nominal rate minus inflation for modest rates.
cards.example: A 5 percent nominal rate with 2 percent inflation implies roughly a 3 percent real rate.

cards.front: What is fiscal policy?
cards.back: Government choices about spending and taxation that influence the economy.
cards.example: A government changes purchases or taxes to affect aggregate demand.

cards.back: Fiscal policy: Government choices about spending and taxation that influence the economy.

cards.front: What is monetary policy?
cards.back: Central-bank actions influencing monetary and financial conditions, such as policy interest rates.
cards.example: A central bank adjusts its policy rate to influence borrowing and spending.

cards.front: What is budget deficit?
cards.back: The amount by which government spending exceeds its revenue during a period.
cards.example: A government spends more this year than it collects this year.

cards.front: Which economic concept does this illustrate? A government spends more this year than it collects this year.
cards.back: Budget deficit: The amount by which government spending exceeds its revenue during a period.

cards.front: What is public debt?
cards.back: The accumulated outstanding borrowing obligations of government, measured at a point in time.
cards.example: Past borrowing remains outstanding even when this year's budget is balanced.
